A Theory Piece · Consumer Psychology & Culture

They Weren't
Made For Us

How hip-hop took luxury brands that were never meant for Black consumers and turned them into the most powerful advertising engine those brands had ever seen

Leon Telemaque · 2026 · Consumer Psychology & Culture · Hip-Hop · Luxury · Early 90s to Present
Run-D.M.C. — the group that turned Adidas into a Black consumer engine before Adidas ever paid them

Music is without a doubt one of the strongest advertisements that has ever existed. Think about it. A 30 second commercial asks you to pay attention. A song asks you for nothing and gives you everything. You hear it while you are driving, while you are in the gym, while you are in the background of a conversation you are barely paying attention to. And somewhere in there, without being asked, you absorb it. You remember it. You feel something about it. No marketing budget in history has replicated that kind of access to a human being. So when the most culturally dominant music genre of the last 30 years started talking about products, those products were going to move. The only question was whether the brands understood what was happening to them.

Most of them did not. At least not at first. And that is the part of the story I find most interesting. Because hip-hop did not set out to be a vehicle for luxury brand adoption. It set out to tell the truth about a community that had been systematically excluded from economic life and the symbols of arrival that economic life produces. The fact that it became the most powerful onboarding mechanism luxury brands have ever had was a consequence nobody designed and almost nobody saw coming.

I. The Brands Were Not Made For Us

You have to start here because it is the foundation of everything else. Gucci, Louis Vuitton, Versace, Cristal, Timberland, Polo Ralph Lauren. None of these brands built their identities with Black consumers in mind. Some of them actively did not want Black consumers. The luxury model specifically was built on exclusivity and the kind of exclusivity that was operating in the early 90s was not just about price. It was about who the brand imagined wearing their product when they designed it. That imagined consumer was not from Compton. Was not from Harlem. Was not from Atlanta.

Luxury brands built their entire model on controlled scarcity and a very specific image of who their consumer was. Hip-hop rewrote that image without asking permission.

And yet. The Notorious B.I.G. wore Versace. Lil Kim wore Gucci. Jay-Z rapped about Cristal like it was the only champagne worth drinking. Damon Dash and Jay-Z were wearing Timberland boots in a way that made an entire generation of kids want them before Timberland had any idea what was happening to their brand in urban markets. Polo Ralph Lauren had been embraced so deeply by Lo-Lifes in Brooklyn that they were shoplifting it wholesale and building an entire subculture around it. The brands were not targeting these consumers. The consumers were claiming the brands.

The psychological move was a reclamation. Taking symbols of a world that had historically excluded you and wearing them as evidence that you had arrived anyway.

This is the part that gets missed in most analyses of hip-hop and luxury. It is framed as aspiration. As Black consumers wanting to look like rich white people. That framing is wrong and it misunderstands the psychology completely. The luxury brand in early 90s hip-hop was not a symbol of wanting to be something else. It was a symbol of having taken something that was not meant for you and making it yours anyway. There is a significant psychological difference between those two things. One is imitation. The other is conquest.

II. The Brands Woke Up Late

For most of the early 90s the brands were confused at best and uncomfortable at worst. Timberland's CEO made public comments about not wanting their boots associated with hip-hop culture. Tommy Hilfiger had rumours circulating for years about comments he allegedly made about not designing for Black consumers. Whether the Tommy Hilfiger story was true or not almost does not matter because the fact that it spread as widely as it did and was believed as widely as it was tells you everything about how Black consumers understood their relationship with these brands. They knew they were not the intended audience. They wore the clothes anyway.

The Cristal moment is the most documented version of this tension. Jay-Z had been rapping about Cristal for years. It was synonymous with hip-hop celebration. Frederic Rouzaud, the managing director of Louis Roederer which makes Cristal, gave an interview in 2006 where he described the hip-hop association as unwanted and said the company could not stop people from buying it. Jay-Z's response was immediate. He pulled Cristal from every venue and event he was associated with and switched to Armand de Brignac. The brand he had been advertising for free for years had revealed how it felt about the consumers driving its cultural relevance. The consumers responded accordingly.

Jay-Z did not just boycott Cristal. He bought a champagne company. That is the difference between a consumer and a builder.

What is psychologically interesting about that moment is not the boycott. Boycotts happen. What is interesting is what came after. Because the Cristal incident made visible something that had been operating under the surface for years. Hip-hop consumers were not passive recipients of brand messaging. They were active co-creators of brand value. They had built Cristal's cultural relevance. They could destroy it just as quickly. And crucially, they were beginning to understand that they had that power.

III. The Collaboration Era

The smarter brands figured out what was happening earlier than the others and moved accordingly. Nike understood it before almost anyone. The Air Jordan line is the first major example of a brand not just tolerating hip-hop's affection but engineering a product specifically for that cultural context. Michael Jordan was not a rapper but he was operating in the same cultural universe and the Air Jordan became one of the most significant consumer objects in hip-hop history without Nike ever making a hip-hop ad. The shoe did the work. The culture did the rest.

By the early 2000s the collaboration model was starting to take shape. Brands were beginning to understand that paying a rapper to mention their product was not as valuable as actually building something with them. The difference between an endorsement and a collaboration is the difference between renting cultural capital and building it. An endorsement gives you access to an artist's audience for a moment. A collaboration gives the artist ownership of the product's meaning and makes the audience feel like they own it too.

Kanye West is the hinge point in this story. His 2009 Louis Vuitton sneaker collaboration was not the first time a rapper had worked with a luxury brand but it was the first time it felt genuinely mutual. Louis Vuitton was not doing Kanye a favour. Kanye was not borrowing Louis Vuitton's prestige. They were building something together that neither could have built alone. The sneakers sold out. The cultural conversation around them was enormous. And it showed the industry that the collaboration model could work at the very highest level of luxury.

IV. Yeezy, Cactus Jack, NOCTA — The Ownership Era

The most significant shift in the relationship between hip-hop and consumer culture is not the collaboration era. The collaboration era was still operating within somebody else's framework. The artist was a creative input into a brand that somebody else owned. The ownership era is something different. It is the point where hip-hop artists stopped being the most powerful advertising mechanism in the world for other people's brands and started being the brand.

Yeezy is the clearest example. What Kanye built with Adidas was not a collaboration in the traditional sense. It was a brand within a brand. Yeezy had its own aesthetic language, its own cultural positioning, its own consumer psychology that was entirely separate from Adidas's existing identity. Adidas was the manufacturing and distribution infrastructure. Yeezy was the brand. The consumers buying Yeezys were not buying Adidas product that Kanye endorsed. They were buying into a cultural universe that Kanye created and Adidas enabled. At its peak Yeezy was generating an estimated 1.5 billion dollars in annual revenue. That is not an endorsement deal. That is a business.

At its peak Yeezy generated an estimated $1.5 billion in annual revenue. That is not an endorsement deal. That is a business built entirely on cultural capital.

Travis Scott's Cactus Jack is a different model but operating on the same principle. Where Yeezy was a fashion brand Cactus Jack is more of a cultural umbrella. The Nike and Jordan Brand collaborations under the Cactus Jack name do not just sell shoes. They sell access to a specific cultural identity. The reverse Nike swoosh on the Air Jordan 1 is one of the most recognisable design choices in sneaker history not because it is objectively better than the regular swoosh but because of what it means to own it. It means you were paying attention. It means you are part of the conversation. Travis Scott did not build a product. He built a membership.

NOCTA is the most interesting of the three from a consumer psychology perspective because it reveals how completely the dynamic has inverted. Drake partnered with Nike to create NOCTA not as a celebrity endorser but as a creative director building a brand that reflects a specific lifestyle and aesthetic. The clothes are not expensive. The positioning is not luxury in the traditional sense. What NOCTA sells is cultural proximity to Drake's world and the specific identity that world represents. That is a much more sophisticated understanding of consumer psychology than anything a traditional brand has historically been able to execute. Drake understands that his audience does not just want his products. They want to feel like they are part of his story.

V. What This Actually Is

When I look at this full arc from Biggie in Versace to Travis Scott reversing the Nike swoosh what I see is a complete consumer psychology story that most marketing textbooks have not caught up to yet. It is the story of a community that was excluded from the production of cultural symbols, claimed those symbols anyway, built enormous value around them, got burned by the brands that benefited, and responded by becoming the brands themselves.

The consumer psychology principle underneath all of it is that authenticity is the most valuable thing a brand can have and authenticity cannot be manufactured. It can only be earned or borrowed. Luxury brands in the early 90s had authenticity with a specific kind of European heritage consumer. Hip-hop gave them something they could not have built themselves which was authenticity with a global youth audience that was going to define consumer culture for the next 30 years. The brands that understood this and responded with genuine collaboration rather than reluctant tolerance ended up on the right side of history. The brands that revealed their discomfort with who was buying their products lost the thing that was making those products matter.

The Full Arc — Five Stages
  1. The organic era (early 90s) — the community claims luxury brands that were not made for them. The brands benefit without understanding why.
  2. The tension era (mid 90s to early 2000s) — brands reveal their discomfort. Timberland, Tommy Hilfiger, Cristal. The community responds with boycotts and redirection.
  3. The endorsement era (early 2000s) — brands start paying for what was previously free. The organic endorsement becomes a transaction. Some authenticity is lost in the exchange.
  4. The collaboration era (mid 2000s to 2010s) — smarter brands move from endorsement to genuine creative partnership. Nike and Jordan, Kanye and Louis Vuitton, Virgil Abloh at Off-White. The artist becomes a co-creator not just a spokesperson.
  5. The ownership era (2010s to present) — Yeezy, Cactus Jack, NOCTA. The community stops building equity for other people's brands and starts building their own. The most powerful advertising engine in consumer history turns inward.

The thing I keep coming back to is Virgil Abloh. He was the creative director of Louis Vuitton men's wear and the founder of Off-White. He was a Black man from Rockford, Illinois who became the most influential figure in luxury fashion of his generation. And the way he got there was not by abandoning the cultural context that shaped him. He brought it with him. He put quotation marks on the word "shoelaces" on a pair of sneakers and the whole industry had to reckon with what he was saying about the arbitrary nature of luxury's value system. He was not asking luxury to accept hip-hop. He was showing luxury that the values it claimed to represent, creativity, craftsmanship, cultural relevance, had already moved.

That is the full story. The brands were not made for us. We wore them anyway. We made them matter in ways they could not make themselves matter. Some of them thanked us and some of them showed us exactly what they thought of us. And then we stopped waiting for their permission and started building something that did not need it.

Music does not ask you to pay attention. It just plays. And while it plays it moves products, builds brands, and rewrites the rules of who consumer culture is actually made for. Hip-hop did not infiltrate luxury. It inherited it.
